{{Short description|An association or meeting of an association}}{{One source|date=August 2026}}

The Japanese term {{Nihongo|2=講|3='''kō'''}} is a general term for an association or organization, as well as a religious term used for the services and gatherings held by such an association.

It originally referred to collections of [[Bhikkhu|monks]] who would gather in temples to analyze and research [[Buddhist texts]], but eventually expanded to include Buddhist services, particularly those involving the recitation of Buddhist texts.<ref name="fukuta-2006a">{{Cite book |last=Sekiguchi |first=Hiō |title=結社の世界史 (1) |publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha |year=2006 |isbn=4-634-44410-0 |edition=1-han |pages=81–96 |oclc=70801976|language=ja|trans-title=A World History of Associations 1|editor-last=Fukuta|editor-first=Ajio|chapter=講と日待|trans-chapter=Kō and Himachi}}</ref> From this, the term expanded further to include [[folk religion]] services and the associations that hold them, and then later to include certain types of mutual aid organizations and associations.

== Original meaning and evolution ==
[[File:2016-09-09_Dorogawa-Onsen,_Tenkawa,_Nara,洞川温泉_DSCF0600.jpg|right|thumb|260x260px|''[[Chōchin]]'' paper lanterns at the front of a {{Transliteration|ja|[[ryokan]]}} at Dorogawa Onsen, located at the foot of [[Mount Ōmine]], with {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} in the name.]]
During the [[Heian period]], the Buddhist school of [[Tiantai]] gained popularity among the Japanese aristocracy who would hold lavish events referred to as {{Nihongo|2=法華八講|3=hokke hakkō|4=lit. "Lotus Sutra eight ''kō''"}} in which the eight scrolls of the [[Lotus Sutra]] were read over a period of four days. This spurred the development of religious gatherings not focused on the study of Buddhist scripture among non-monks, such as the [[Hōonkō]].<ref name="fukuta-2006a" /> As these {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} spread through society during the medieval period, many religious organizations were formed with the term {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} in the name. These religious organizations included those that formed naturally within local communities as well as those that were introduced from outside.

The former type of {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} were operated by {{Transliteration|ja|[[ujiko]]|}} (shrine parishioners) to maintain the [[Shinto shrine|shrines]] of the local {{Transliteration|ja|[[ujigami]]}} or {{Transliteration|ja|[[ubusunagami]]}} they worshipped. The {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} of high-ranking shrines were formed of members from a wide range, far beyond the scope of the village the shrine was located in. {{Transliteration|ja|Kō}} grew more powerful during the [[Sengoku period]] as the {{Nihongo|2=講元|3=kōmoto}}, the head of a {{Transliteration|ja|kō}}, was granted {{Transliteration|ja|[[jizamurai]]}} status or selected from an existing {{Nihongo|2=国人|3=kokunin|4=locals of particular power such as village heads}} or {{Transliteration|ja|jizamurai}}. The [[Kaga ikki|Kaga ''ikki'']] was run by a {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} of [[Jōdo Shinshū]] Buddhists. 

As an organization, {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} were operated on a semi-democratic basis. The {{Transliteration|ja|kō}}, also called {{Nihongo|2=講社|3=kōsha}}, was formed of members called {{Nihongo|2=講員|3=kōin}}. The various positions, {{Transliteration|ja|kōmoto}}, {{Nihongo|2=副講元|3=fuku-kōmoto|4=assistant ''kō'' chief}}, and {{Nihongo|2=世話人|3=sawanin|4=lit. “carer”}} were often elected from among the members or assigned by the temple or shrine the {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} worshipped at. For more local customs such as worship of mountain {{Transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} and {{Transliteration|ja|[[chinjugami]]}}, family and territorial units formed the membership of a {{Transliteration|ja|kō}}, preventing the organization from being solely religious in nature.<ref name="fukuta-2006a" />

Initially, the latter form of {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} introduced from outside the local community had their origins in [[mountain worship]]. The [[Shugendō]] practitioners of mountains such as [[Mount Tate]] traveled Japan forming {{Nihongo|2=参拝講|3=sanpai-kō|4="pilgrimage ''kō''"}} encouraging others to climb holy mountains. Shrines and [[Buddhist temple|temples]] around Japan imitated this practice and established {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} in order to draw in worshippers. In some cases, all members of these {{Transliteration|ja|sanpai-kō}} would travel to the shrine or temple, but, in others, a number of the members were selected as representatives to travel to the shrine or temple and worship there on behalf of their fellows. The evolution of {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} as [[mutual aid]] organizations such as {{Transliteration|ja|[[tanomoshiko]]}} began with these representative pilgrimages. Rather than each member contributing money to fund a pilgrimage, members would each contribute funds which were then lent to a member chosen either by lottery or through applications. In addition to religious {{Transliteration|ja|kō}}, there were a large variety of groups such as {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} for workers in the same field ([[Moai (social support groups)|moai-kō]] and [[Yui (behavior)|yui-kō]]) and {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} for people of the same gender or of similar ages ({{Nihongo|2=若衆講|3=wakaishu-kō|4=youth ''kō''}} and {{Nihongo|2=カカ講|3=kaka-kō|4=Mom ''kō''}}).<ref name="fukuta-2006a" /> While these {{Transliteration|ja|kō}} primarily required members to pay money into the group, there were some free to join whose primary function was recreation, such as {{Nihongo|2=遊山講|3=yusan-kō|4=picnic ''kō''}} which were usually social groups for women.
